parts.title: Finding a rental property
parts.transcript:
Narrator: IELTS listening. Version 18134.

Narrator: There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions and you will have a chance to check your work.
Narrator: All the recordings will be played once only.
Narrator: The test is in four sections.
Narrator: Write all your answers in the listening question booklet.
Narrator: At the end of the test, you will be given 10 minutes to transfer your answers to an answer sheet.
Narrator: Now turn to section one on page two of your question booklet.
Narrator: Section one.
Narrator: You will hear a telephone conversation between a woman called Susan, who is looking for accommodation to rent, and a real estate agent.

parts.title: Preschool Family Center introduction
parts.transcript:
Narrator: Section two.
Narrator: You will hear an introductory talk to a group of parents about a special center for young children.
Narrator: First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14 on page three.
Narrator: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
Speaker 1: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the Preschool Family Center.
Speaker 1: It's really good to see so many parents here, and I hope this talk will help you to find out more about what we do here and how the center works, so you can decide if this sounds the right sort of place for your child.
Speaker 1: Okay, so first of all, what is the Preschool Family Center?
Speaker 1: Well, basically, it's a childhood education center for children from three months up to five years old.
Speaker 1: But we're different from a lot of other organizations for preschool children.
Speaker 1: We believe that the first educators of a child are their parents.
Speaker 1: And so, the Preschool Family Center is organized as a cooperative by the parents, which means it is the parents themselves who are responsible for running the center, and also for running each session.
Speaker 1: So this means that we ask parents to attend the center with their children on a regular basis.
Speaker 1: In order to make this work, we offer training for parents, teaching them the skills they need to work with children and run the sessions.
Speaker 1: The children do all sorts of different activities: art, music, singing, and games.
Speaker 1: And these are all done in groups of mixed ages, because we believe that by learning to play together, children learn how to make choices, and how to respect people and things.
Narrator: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20 on page three.
Narrator: Now, listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
Speaker 1: Now, some factual information.
Speaker 1: Sessions run each morning from 9:30 to 12:30, and we have an extra session on Thursday afternoons, which is solely for older children, where we do some activities to help prepare them for reading before they start school.
Speaker 1: We feel this is really important, and can make a big difference when they get to school.
Speaker 1: And now, before you enroll your child in the center, you need to make at least five visits with your child.
Speaker 1: This is so you are fully aware of how the center works before you enroll.
Speaker 1: The centers are recognized as official preschools, and so each center is entitled to funding from the government.
Speaker 1: The center is a really wonderful experience, but does require some work.
Speaker 1: So I'd just like to talk about some of the commitments you will need to make, if you decide to go ahead and enroll your child.
Speaker 1: A couple of points first.
Speaker 1: Once you and your child have settled into the center and are familiar with how things work, you will be asked to choose a particular job, like secretary, or gardener, or librarian, or something to be responsible for.
Speaker 1: And, we have a meeting which we use to plan the program, and each parent is expected to attend this.
Speaker 1: Now, just before we move on to answer any questions you have, I'd just quickly like to mention some of the ways you and your child are able to get the most out of the center.
Speaker 1: It's important that you attend regularly.
Speaker 1: This way, you'll get to know other parents well, and your child will develop confidence while he or she is here.
Speaker 1: Younger children might need to leave early.
Speaker 1: It's better to leave early than to go home with an overtired child.
Speaker 1: We do provide drinks for the children, but we ask you to make sure your child has a snack to eat during the morning.
Speaker 1: No crisps or chocolate, please.
Speaker 1: Right, I think I'll stop there and ask if anyone's got any questions.
Narrator: That is the end of section two.
Narrator: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
Narrator: Now turn to section three on page four.

parts.transcript:
Narrator: Section three.
Narrator: You will hear two sports physiotherapy students called John and Kath, preparing a joint presentation on foot injuries in sports players.
Narrator: First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26 on page four.
Narrator: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 26.
Speaker 1: I've had a look at your draft presentation plan and compared it with mine, Kath, and we seem to have the same basic structure.
Speaker 1: We've both included the same three main sections, that's the anatomy of the foot, the injuries and the treatment, and we've organized our presentations in the same way.
Speaker 1: But the types of sports we've chosen to illustrate the possible injuries aren't the same.
Speaker 2: I'll deal with the anatomy bit.
Speaker 2: I've got notes in a handout on that from Professor Gilligan's lecture.
Speaker 1: Oh, I was hoping to do that.
Speaker 1: I've downloaded some useful stuff.
Speaker 1: I do think we should limit this section though.
Speaker 1: We don't want to spend much time on anatomy when the main focus is on the treatment.
Speaker 2: That's true, but in the last section, maybe the two of us could show how some of these therapies actually work.
Speaker 2: I could be the patient and you could do the treatment.
Speaker 1: Hmm, good idea, because it's hard to find pictures as injuries are mostly internal.
Speaker 1: It would be good to hear some first-hand accounts from injured athletes too.
Speaker 2: Yeah, but we don't have time.
Speaker 1: No.
Speaker 1: Should we then discuss different types of heel injury?
Speaker 1: It's worth pointing out that these vary enormously in how bad they are.
Speaker 1: It might be just a pulled muscle, or a bone injury which needs surgery.
Speaker 1: Sometimes only an expert can tell the difference.
Speaker 2: Excellent.
Speaker 2: I'll do the slides on that.
Speaker 2: Leave that one to me.
Speaker 1: Now, what about causes of heel injuries?
Speaker 2: Well, it's easy enough to list them, overuse, improper footwear.
Speaker 1: Yes, um, incorrect running style.
Speaker 2: They're all relevant, but for simplicity, let's just pick one cause.
Speaker 2: Say, stuff about changing your training habits suddenly.
Speaker 1: You mean like suddenly doing a lot of mountain training?
Speaker 1: Yes.
Speaker 1: That's a good idea.
Speaker 1: And there was research on that in the latest edition of Physio Journal, wasn't there?
Speaker 1: Professor Gilligan recommended it to us.
Speaker 2: Great.
Speaker 2: Uh, you can leave the bit on stretching techniques to me.
Speaker 2: I really like all that stuff.
Speaker 1: So, what's going to be your approach there?
Speaker 2: Well, I'll summarize all the various techniques with visual support, and then I'll make the point that the stretching should be carefully managed.
Speaker 2: Obviously, you have to be careful not to overstretch, and to stretch only when your muscles are warmed up.
Speaker 2: Otherwise you could do yourself more harm than good.
Speaker 2: It's also important that on a supervised program, stretching is later on combined with balance exercises, which stretch and also strengthen the muscles.
Speaker 1: Okay then.
Narrator: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30 on page five.
Narrator: Now listen and answer questions 27 to 30.
Speaker 1: It's always useful to have some information on case studies at the end, in case we're short of material.
Speaker 1: Did you manage to find anything?
Speaker 2: Yes, a female runner in her 30s, talking about her treatment for a swollen heel.
Speaker 2: Initially, she rested the injury.
Speaker 2: This did help to reduce the swelling, although it was still a little bit uncomfortable.
Speaker 2: Then she applied an ice pack to the injury twice a day.
Speaker 1: Did that work?
Speaker 2: Well, she persisted with this treatment for the first month, but decided it wasn't helping.
Speaker 2: After this period, she was shown how to use deep tissue massage techniques, and was surprised at how much freedom of movement this created in her foot.
Speaker 1: Wasn't she having ultrasound treatment?
Speaker 2: Yes, she was having sessions at the hospital, but she remained unconvinced about its value.
Speaker 2: She felt the same about the balancing exercises she was prescribed.
Speaker 1: Okay, that's interesting.
Speaker 1: I looked at the aftercare program of a male sprinter who was allowed to do some sports activity as part of his rehabilitation.
Speaker 1: After four months of treatment, he did some light running on grass, wearing shoes that gave plenty of support to his injured heel.
Speaker 2: So, it didn't hurt?
Speaker 1: Well, he found the heel was sore afterwards, and the same happened with some jumping exercises he was asked to try.
Speaker 2: Did he go to the gym and use weights?
Speaker 1: Yes, after a few weeks, and if he used lightweight, he could train without pain.
Speaker 1: He also tried cycling and found this beneficial, as his foot was not making contact with the ground.
Speaker 1: He expected a similar result with swimming, but found the repetitive kicking motion was actually aggravating the injury.
Speaker 2: Well, both these case studies have value.
Narrator: That is the end of section three.
Narrator: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
Narrator: Now turn to section four on page six.

parts.transcript:
Narrator: Section four.
Narrator: You will hear part of a lecture on the ways that supermarkets use layout to increase sales.
Narrator: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40 on pages six and seven.
Narrator: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
Speaker 1: We've been looking at marketing techniques which influence buying decisions.
Speaker 1: Some of these techniques are related to the way the products are presented in the store.
Speaker 1: For supermarkets, the store layout is not as random as it seems.
Speaker 1: Decisions have to be made about the arrangement of the aisles where the customers walk, and the shelves and so on, where the products are displayed.
Speaker 1: The most common layout pattern is the grid layout, where parallel aisles are arranged in a rectangular pattern.
Speaker 1: Supermarkets like this layout as it allows them to utilize floor space efficiently by providing the greatest amount of display space proportionate to aisle space.
Speaker 1: Also, this layout helps to manage traffic flow, as it encourages people to all walk in one direction.
Speaker 1: The main weaknesses of the grid layout are the monotony of rows of aisles, and the fact that it is easier for customers to rush through the supermarket without lingering.
Speaker 1: Another layout pattern used by supermarkets is known as the free form.
Speaker 1: Here, displays and aisles are arranged in a random pattern.
Speaker 1: The good thing about this layout is that customers tend to spend more time in the store as they wander about looking for different products.
Speaker 1: Its main weakness is the inefficient use of space, which means it is less cost effective.
Speaker 1: Then we have the boutique layout, where everything is organized around a food specialty, such as the bakery.
Speaker 1: The advantage of this layout is that it divides parts of the store into smaller areas, which may be distinguished by changes in flooring or displays.
Speaker 1: A further advantage is that this style of layout is attractive to shoppers.
Speaker 1: Space, however, is not used economically, and it is therefore expensive.
Speaker 1: The choice of location of particular types of items in the store is also important.
Speaker 1: A supermarket's design aims to direct customers to the store's side and rear walls.
Speaker 1: Items typically displayed along the rear length of the store include meat and dairy products, since these appear on the grocery list of the majority of shoppers.
Speaker 1: This means shoppers must pass by a large number of other items to get to them.
Speaker 1: Items which consumers tend to spend more time considering before buying, such as cosmetics, are usually placed away from the busy areas, so that people can look at them in comfort, without feeling rushed.
Speaker 1: Products placed at the end of aisles are clearly visible, and therefore these locations provide a greater opportunity for shoppers to view the products.
Speaker 1: Consumers tend to assume that items on display at the end of an aisle are on sale, but this is often not the case.
Speaker 1: In fact, supermarket managers often place products which are not selling quickly enough in these positions.
Speaker 1: The placement of products on shelves is very carefully planned.
Speaker 1: Supermarket executives use computer-generated plans to help them place products on shelves in a way that ensures consumers spend more.
Speaker 1: The eye level of the average woman is 1m 60 cm off the floor, which is the height of the middle shelves.
Speaker 1: So the things which cost more are placed here, while cheaper products are placed on higher or lower shelves.
Speaker 1: Only items targeted at children break this rule.
Speaker 1: They are placed on the lowest shelves.
Speaker 1: Supermarkets also use a range of other marketing techniques to encourage consumers to spend more.
Speaker 1: It's no accident that in nearly every supermarket, the fruit and vegetable department is the first shoppers come to as they enter the store.
Speaker 1: These, together with flowers, produce a greater profit than any other department.
Speaker 1: After complaints from parents, many supermarkets no longer place popular products aimed at children on the shelves next to the checkout.
Speaker 1: Instead, you are most likely to find products aimed at impulse buyers, such as chocolate, magazines, and other treats here.
Speaker 1: Many supermarkets have also expanded into non-food areas such as clothing, entertainment and stationary.
Speaker 1: These products often find...
